summary: Describes a dynamic way for IS-IS routers to learn symbolic hostnames, using a TLV that floods each router's name-to-system-ID mapping across the network. This makes logs and commands easier to read than raw system IDs. It obsoleted RFC 2763 and moved the capability onto the standards track. It was updated later by RFC 6232.

eli5.summary: Computers use numbers, but people like names. This lets routers tell each other their names, so humans can read network reports more easily without decoding long strings of numbers.

questions: how routers learn names in is-is
what is the is-is dynamic hostname tlv
how do is-is routers learn hostnames
subtitle: A way for IS-IS routers to advertise their own names, so people can read network output without decoding system IDs.

tldr.problem: IS-IS identifies routers by system IDs, which are hard to read in diagnostics, and keeping a hand-built table of names on every router does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: Each router puts its own symbolic name in an optional Dynamic hostname TLV (type 137) in its link state PDUs, and other routers can learn the name-to-system-ID mapping from the flooded LSPs.
tldr.outcome: Operators get readable names without static tables or DNS. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2763 and moves the mechanism to the Standards Track; RFC 6232 later updated it.

today: RFC 5301 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2763 and has been updated by RFC 6232. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Names Are Needed
sections.content:
IS-IS uses a variable system ID of 1 to 8 bytes (normally 6 bytes) to identify each node. When operators check adjacencies, routing table entries or the link state database, hexadecimal system IDs and LSP identifiers are less clear than symbolic names.

A name-to-system-ID mapping can be used both ways: to find the name for an ID and the ID for a name. Common practice among IS-IS operators was to configure such mappings statically.
sections.eli5: Imagine a class list that only has ID numbers. It is much easier to read when each number has a name next to it.

sections.title: Possible Solutions
sections.content:
Static tables need an entry for every router on every router. Renaming a router, changing its system ID or adding a new one affects the configuration of all the others, so the tables are very likely to go out of date.

A central table in DNS would help, but DNS response time may be poor or the service unavailable during network problems. DNS also adds complexity, and some implementations might not support A and PTR records for CLNS NSAPs.

The third option, which this document defines, uses the routing protocol's own transport: a new TLV lets routers include the mapping in their LSPs. The RFC says this gives simple and reliable transport of name information, and that in wide-scale deployment it proved easier and more manageable than static mapping or DNS.
sections.eli5: You could write every name on every kid's notebook by hand, or ask the office down the hall. It is easier if each kid just wears a name tag.

sections.title: The Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
The Dynamic hostname TLV is TLV type 137. Its Length is the total length of the value field, and its Value is a string of 1 to 255 bytes. The string is not null-terminated.

The TLV is optional and may be present in any fragment of a non-pseudonode LSP. The value is the symbolic name of the router that originated the LSP. It can be the FQDN, a subset of it, or any string the operator wants, although using the FQDN or a subset is strongly recommended. The router's system ID can be derived from the LSP identifier.

The value is encoded in 7-bit ASCII. If a user interface accepts or shows Unicode, that interface is responsible for applying the ToASCII and ToUnicode algorithms from RFC 3490.
sections.eli5: The name tag is a small box in the router's message that holds a short piece of plain text with the router's name.

sections.title: How Routers Use It
sections.content:
Including the TLV is the originating router's choice. A router that receives an LSP with the TLV may ignore it, or may install the name and system ID in its hostname mapping table for the IS-IS network.

If a router receives a mapping for a name or system ID that differs from its cached one, it SHOULD replace the existing mapping with the latest information.

A router may also insert the TLV in its pseudonode LSP to associate a symbolic name with a local LAN. If the TLV appears in a pseudonode LSP, it SHOULD NOT be interpreted as the DNS hostname of the router.
sections.eli5: When a router sees a new name tag it can write it down or ignore it. If a tag changes, it crosses out the old one and uses the newest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mappings come from the routers themselves, so a misconfigured or compromised router can inject false ones. The RFC says the information must be treated with suspicion, for example when doing diagnostics about a suspected security incident.

It raises no other new security issues for IS-IS. Security issues with IS-IS are discussed in RFC 5304.
sections.eli5: A name tag is only as honest as the person wearing it. A router could wear a fake one, so do not trust names too much when investigating a problem.
